scenes.tts: A mixture of plant species can outyield its monocultures. Does it do so for one reason, or for two? Take a made-up example. Two species are sown in equal proportions. Species A alone yields four hundred grams of dry biomass per square metre. Species B alone yields one hundred. Sown together, they yield four hundred. Is that a gain, and where does it come from?
scenes.caption: A mixture of plant species can outyield its monocultures. Does it do so for one reason, or for two? Take a made-up example. Two species are sown in equal proportions. Species A alone yields 400 grams of dry biomass per square metre. Species B alone yields 100. Sown together, they yield 400. Is that a gain, and where does it come from?
scenes.visual: Bars: A alone 400, B alone 100, and a stacked mixture bar (A 300 + B 100) with a dashed question-mark gap above the average
scenes.narration: A mixture of plant species can outyield its monocultures. Does it do so for one reason, or for two? Take a made-up example. Two species are sown in equal proportions. Species A alone yields 400 grams of dry biomass per square metre. Species B alone yields 100. Sown together, they yield 400. Is that a gain, and where does it come from?

scenes.tts: First, set a benchmark. The expected mixture yield is the mean of the two monocultures. Four hundred plus one hundred, over two, is two hundred fifty. The observed yield is four hundred. The net effect is the difference: plus one hundred fifty grams per square metre. That gain has two parts.
scenes.caption: First, set a benchmark. The expected mixture yield is the mean of the two monocultures. (400 + 100)/2 = 250. The observed yield is 400. The net effect is the difference: +150 grams per square metre. That gain has two parts.
scenes.visual: Dashed expected line at 250 across the bars; gold bracket from 250 to 400 labelled +150; bracket splits into two
scenes.narration: First, set a benchmark. The expected mixture yield is the mean of the two monocultures. (400 + 100)/2 = 250. The observed yield is 400. The net effect is the difference: +150 grams per square metre. That gain has two parts.

scenes.tts: Complementarity is the first part. On average, species do better in mixture than their monocultures predict, as they would if they used resources differently or helped one another. Selection is the second part. A random mix is more likely to include one highly productive species, and that species dominates. The partition measures both.

scenes.visual: Two panels: complementarity (two dots each stepping up past their expected mark) and selection (a random draw of dots where one large productive dot takes over); then net = complementarity + selection
scenes.narration: Complementarity is the first part. On average, species do better in mixture than their monocultures predict, as they would if they used resources differently or helped one another. Selection is the second part. A random mix is more likely to include one highly productive species, and that species dominates. The partition measures both.

scenes.tts: Now measure each species against its own monoculture. Species A yields three hundred in the mixture, out of four hundred alone. Its relative yield is zero point seven five. Species B yields one hundred, out of one hundred alone. Its relative yield is one. Each was sown at half, so each was expected at zero point five. The gains are zero point two five and zero point five.
scenes.caption: Now measure each species against its own monoculture. Species A yields 300 in the mixture, out of 400 alone. Its relative yield is 0.75. Species B yields 100, out of 100 alone. Its relative yield is 1. Each was sown at half, so each was expected at 0.5. The gains are 0.25 and 0.5.
scenes.visual: Two relative-yield bars (A 0.75, B 1.00) against a dashed expected 0.5 line; gain brackets 0.25 and 0.50
scenes.narration: Now measure each species against its own monoculture. Species A yields 300 in the mixture, out of 400 alone. Its relative yield is 0.75. Species B yields 100, out of 100 alone. Its relative yield is 1. Each was sown at half, so each was expected at 0.5. The gains are 0.25 and 0.5.

scenes.tts: Complementarity is richness times the mean gain times the mean monoculture yield. Two times zero point three seven five times two hundred fifty is plus one hundred eighty-seven point five. Selection asks whether the species with high monoculture yields gained most. Here the larger gain went to species B, the low yielder. So selection is negative: minus thirty-seven point five. Add them, and you get one hundred fifty, the net effect.
scenes.caption: Complementarity is richness times the mean gain times the mean monoculture yield. 2 × 0.375 × 250 is +187.5. Selection asks whether the species with high monoculture yields gained most. Here the larger gain went to species B, the low yielder. So selection is negative: −37.5. Add them, and you get 150, the net effect.
scenes.visual: Waterfall: green +187.5 bar, red -37.5 step back, gold net 150 total, with the equations written beside it
scenes.narration: Complementarity is richness times the mean gain times the mean monoculture yield. 2 × 0.375 × 250 is +187.5. Selection asks whether the species with high monoculture yields gained most. Here the larger gain went to species B, the low yielder. So selection is negative: −37.5. Add them, and you get 150, the net effect.

scenes.tts: Last, compare with the best monoculture. The mixture yields four hundred, exactly what species A yields alone. So there is no transgressive overyielding. The mixture beats the average monoculture, but not the best. Also, a positive complementarity term does not prove resource partitioning. Keep this rule: the partition splits the gain, but it names no mechanism.
